It's common because it's simple, but it's also a crappy question because it misrepresents the process for how political philosophy translates into actual policy and governance. Principles do not flow backwards out of a grand narrative describing a perfect utopian society and a hopeful story about how these certain principles will take us there. They aren't a guide to a destination, they're fuel in the tank. Principles have value in and of themselves regardless of our ability to predict how a society focused on them will decide to deal with any particular issue.

This sort of discussion also does nothing to strengthen or undermine what society can gain by finding opportunities to insert libertarian ideals into policy. If we're asserting digital privacy rights, legalizing marijuana, and stopping campus crackdowns on offensive/dissenting speech today, then we'll be better off tomorrow. I try to focus on this principle-driven approach to good governance, but there's no reason it can't co-exist with a debate regarding the best response to the "who builds roads in libertarian utopia" question.
